title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $F\subset \Gamma\backslash \textup{Rad}(\Gamma)$ be finite. There are subsets $A_n\subset B_n$ of \hbox{exponential} growth such that the maps $
A_n\ni a\mapsto aga^{-1}$
are injective, for all $g\in F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We proceed by induction. If $g\in \Gamma\backslash \textup{Rad}(\Gamma)$, then find elements $t_1, ..., t_m\in \Gamma$ such that the subgroup $H = \langle t_kgt_k^{-1}: 1\leq k \leq m\rangle\leq\Gamma$ is nonamenable. Let $B_k(H)$ denote the ball of radius $k$ in $H$, with respect to this generating set, and consider the well-defined injective map
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{Q}: H/Z(H)\ni hZ(H)\mapsto (ht_1gt_1^{-1}h^{-1}, ..., ht_mgt_m^{-1}h^{-1}).
\end{align*}
Because $H/Z(H)$ is nonamenable, it has exponential growth, and therefore $\mathcal{Q}(B_k(H))\subset \prod_{k=1}^m H$ has exponential growth. It follows (from e.g., the pigeonhole principle), that there is $1\leq k_0\leq m$ such that the subset $\{st_{k_0}gt_{k_0}^{-1}s^{-1}: s\in B_n(H)\}$ has exponential growth in $H$, and therefore $\{tgt^{-1}: t\in B_n\}$ has exponential growth in $\Gamma$. This proves the base case $|F| = 1$.

Now suppose the theorem is proven for subsets $F\subset \Gamma$ of cardinality $|F| < m$, and consider $m$
distinct elements $g_1, ..., g_m\in \Gamma\backslash \textup{Rad}(\Gamma).$ Let $A_n\subset B_n$ be a sequence of subsets with exponential growth such that the maps
               
$A_n\ni a\mapsto ag_ka^{-1}$
             
are injective, for all $k < m$. Consider the number of fibers $\iota(n)$ for the maps $\pi_n: A_n\ni a\mapsto aC_\Gamma(g_m)\in \Gamma/C_{\Gamma}(g_m)$. 
If there is a strictly increasing sequence $(n_k)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ with $\iota(n_k) \sim \alpha^{n_k}$ for some $\alpha > 1$, we are done. 
If not, then for each $n$ there is a fiber, say $A_n\supset A_n' = \pi_n^{-1}(\{x_n\})$ for $x_n\in A_n$, of exponential growth. We will use $A_n'$ to construct a new subset $A_n''\subset B_{3n}$ with the property that the maps $A_n''\ni a\mapsto aC_\Gamma(g_k)$ are injective, for every $k = 1, ..., m$, and this will complete the proof. We will do this with a diagonalization argument. Let $f(n) = \min\{|A_n'|, |q_m(B_n)|\}$ (where $q_m: \Gamma\to \Gamma/C_\Gamma(g_m)$ is the coset map), and enumerate $A_n' = \{a_1, ..., a_{P(n)}\}$, $q_m(B_n) = \{b_1, ..., b_{Q(n)}\}$. The functions $P(n)$, $Q(n)$, and $f(n)$ have exponential growth.
Find $N\in\mathbb{N}$ with $f(n)> 2m$ for all $n > N$, and now fix such $n$. Consider the $Q(n)$ subsets $b_1x_n^{-1}A'_n, b_2x_n^{-1}A'_n, ..., b_{Q(n)}x_{n}^{-1}A'_n$. We construct $A_n''$ inductively: suppose that $\ell-1$ elements $y_i\in b_ix_n^{-1}A_n'$ ($i <\ell < f(n)/2m$) have been chosen with distinct $C_{\Gamma}(g_k)$-cosets for all $k = 1, ..., m$. We choose the $\ell$th element of $A_n''$ by removing all elements from $b_{\ell}x_{n}^{-1}A_n''$ which share a $C_{\Gamma}(g_k)$-coset with some $y_i$, for $i < \ell$ and $k < m$ (there are at most $\ell m$ such elements), and choosing an element from the remaining set (such an element exists by the choice of $N$).
Because $n > N$, this process may be continued $f(n)/2m$ times, so that $A_n''$ is a set of cardinality $f(n)/2m$ 
for which all $m$ conjugation maps are injective. This completes step $|F| = m$.
